title: Systems Design Assessment
description: Eight trading-systems design questions covering deterministic replay, feed normalisation, delivery semantics, uncertain order status, latency, data bias, tick storage and reconciliation. Allow about three minutes per question. Some answers require several distinct mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Sketch the design of a price-time-priority matching engine: what data structures hold the order book, what invariant must hold after every processed event, and why must the engine's event application be deterministic and replayable?
questions.modelAnswer: Per side of the book, keep a price-ordered structure (a balanced tree / sorted map of price levels, or a heap keyed by price) holding FIFO queues of orders at each level, the tree gives fast best-bid/ask access and level insertion, the queues give time priority. Invariant: after every incoming event the book must not be crossed (best bid < best ask); matching logic generates trades precisely to restore that invariant, and each event application is a pure, deterministic transformation so replaying the recorded event stream from a snapshot reproduces the exact book state and trade sequence, which is what makes debugging, dispute resolution and disaster recovery possible.
questions.explanation: Two structures cooperate: order across price levels (tree/heap/sorted map) and order within a level (FIFO queue for time priority). The no-cross invariant is the correctness contract, a crossed book means an executable trade was missed. Determinism matters because the exchange's event log IS the truth: if replaying it reproduces state bit-for-bit, you can audit any historical moment and recover from crashes by replay, without inventing ad-hoc state recovery.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the normalisation stage in a multi-venue market data feed handler?
options: Translate venue encodings and scales into a canonical internal schema
Discard every duplicate without maintaining any ordering or gap state
Compress every packet without interpreting any venue field semantics
Encode strategy orders for outbound transmission to the trading venue
questions.explanation: Each venue speaks its own dialect: different field layouts, integer price scales, side conventions, message taxonomies and clocks (with different latencies and sync quality). Normalisation maps all of it into one internal schema with consistent, corrected timestamps, the single place venue quirks are handled, so the strategy consumes one clean stream. Compression, order routing and dedup are concerns of other stages.

questions.prompt: Why is true exactly-once event processing hard to achieve in a distributed trading system, and what is the standard practical approximation used instead?
questions.modelAnswer: If a consumer crashes between applying an event and acknowledging it, neither retrying (risking a second application) nor skipping (risking a lost event) is safe, achieving exactly-once requires transactional coordination or deduplication machinery on every path, which is expensive and fragile. Standard practice: let the transport guarantee at-least-once delivery (dupes are possible) and make the application itself idempotent, keyed on sequence numbers or dedup IDs, so duplicate deliveries are recognised and ignored. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing yields effectively-once behaviour.
questions.explanation: The impossibility lives in the window between 'did the work' and 'confirmed the work': no message can tell you whether the receiver processed it before dying. Rather than pay for distributed transactions everywhere, systems choose at-least-once (never lose) and push the burden to the consumer, whose sequence-number/dedup-key check turns possible duplicates into harmless no-ops. The same pattern appears in every fill-processing and position-update path.

questions.prompt: An order gateway times out waiting for an exchange acknowledgement. Why is order status uncertain, why can a fresh client order ID duplicate exposure, and how should retry or reconciliation be chosen?
questions.modelAnswer: The first order may already be live despite the missing acknowledgement. A new client order ID may create a second order. Follow the specific venue session and duplicate-ID rules, use a supported status query or reconciliation, and preserve the original intent identity rather than assuming a universal resend guarantee.
questions.explanation: An acknowledgement timeout is not a rejection. Some protocols support idempotent requests, while others require session-level resend or status handling. Reusing an identifier is not universally safe without checking its venue-defined semantics; generating a new ID can duplicate a live order.

questions.prompt: A tick-to-trade latency budget of 5 microseconds must be decomposed across the pipeline. Which decomposition approach is most useful in practice?
options: Split the target equally across components without observing workloads
Measure end-to-end tails and stage distributions with their dependence
Sum one mean per function and treat the sum as the pipeline p99 value
Measure only strategy arithmetic because network and queues are free
questions.explanation: Pipeline latency is a sum of stage times. Percentiles do not generally add or multiply: dependence, queueing and workload determine the end-to-end tail. Instrument both full-path latency and stage distributions; a mean-only budget hides slow events.

questions.prompt: A backtest runs a momentum strategy on today's S&P 500 constituents over the last 20 years of prices. Name the main bias, explain why it inflates results, and give the standard fix.
questions.modelAnswer: Survivorship bias. Today's constituents are precisely the firms that survived 20 years, companies that were delisted, acquired or went bankrupt are excluded, so the backtest universe systematically omits the catastrophic losers a real-time trader would have held. Momentum strategies especially suffer because dead momentum names (crashers) vanish from the sample. Fix: point-in-time universes, rebuild the constituent list as it actually existed on each historical date, including since-removed names (and be equally careful that fundamentals/data used at each date were knowable then, avoiding look-ahead).
questions.explanation: Any backtest built on a list selected using future information inherits a tilted universe. Survivorship inflates returns and understates drawdowns; the cure is reconstructing history as it was known at each point (constituents, listings, corporate actions). It pairs with look-ahead bias, using data at time $t$ that was only published after $t$ - and both are caught by the same discipline: simulate only with information available at decision time.

questions.prompt: Why can an immutable raw tick-event log benefit from append-only, time-ordered, columnar analytical storage, and why should corrections remain distinguishable from the original events?
questions.modelAnswer: Sequential appends preserve an auditable event history. Columnar layout supports scans over selected fields and compression. Corrections can be appended as explicit new events or represented in a separate derived view, rather than silently erasing the raw event history.
questions.explanation: Raw event logs and corrected analytical views serve different purposes. Appending preserves audit and replay, while columnar scans can reduce I/O. Real feeds can contain corrections, so saying all ticks are never revised in every storage layer is too broad.

questions.prompt: At end of day, your internal position for XYZ is 12,400 shares but the clearing report says 12,350. Describe the reconciliation workflow you would run and the root-cause technique for locating the divergence.
questions.modelAnswer: First flag the break and treat the internal position as unreliable until resolved, no trading on an unvalidated book. Reconcile all three ledgers (internal expected positions, venue/clearing records, and the trade history) across positions, cash and transactions. Root-cause by replaying both event streams (orders sent, fills received, cancels, corrections, position transfers) from a common known-good starting snapshot, stepping forward in timestamp order until the states diverge: the first divergent event is the culprit (typically a missed fill report, an unapplied correction, or a duplicate). Then repair the state, document the break and resolution in an audit trail, and harden the process (e.g. missing-message detection) so that class of break is caught intraday next time.
questions.explanation: Reconciliation is a systematic diff, not a shrug: expected vs actual vs history. The replay-to-divergence technique is the general tool for state mismatch, because every system is a deterministic function of its event history, the first event where two replays disagree is necessarily where the bug or missing message lives. Post-trade integrity is what lets a desk trust its own PnL, which is why break handling is treated as a first-class engineering workflow rather than a manual chore.
